nameStory: The name 'brunnea' comes from the Latin word for brown, referring to this tiny spider's earthy coloration. Like many dwarf spiders, it gets its common family name from its incredibly small size - these spiders are so petite they could easily be mistaken for specks of dirt or tiny seeds.
description: The Brown Dwarf Spider is one of New England's tiniest arachnids, belonging to the sheetweb and dwarf weaver family. These minuscule spiders are brownish in color and so small they're easily overlooked by casual observers. Despite their size, they're accomplished web builders, creating delicate sheet webs to catch even smaller prey. They represent some of the most diminutive members of the spider world found in our region.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely tiny - often less than 3mm in body length, smaller than most ants you'd encounter, requiring close inspection or magnification to see details clearly

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded abdomen with a relatively small cephalothorax (front section), giving it a somewhat globular appearance when viewed from above

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Overall brownish coloration that may appear almost amber-like in good light, with subtle variations in shading across the body

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates small, delicate sheet webs close to the ground or in low vegetation, often with a fine, silky texture that catches dew beautifully in morning light

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves quickly when disturbed, often dropping from webs or scurrying to hide under leaves or debris with surprising agility for such a small creature

habitat: Found in leaf litter, low vegetation, and ground-level microhabitats throughout New England's forests and woodland edges. They prefer moist environments with plenty of organic matter where they can hunt tiny insects and other microscopic prey. Look for them in areas with dense ground cover, fallen logs, or mossy patches where humidity levels remain consistent.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to establish territories and rebuild webs damaged by winter weather.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, actively hunting and reproducing, with webs most easily spotted in early morning dew.
seasonality.fall: Mating season occurs, with egg-laying taking place before winter. Adults may still be active on warm autumn days.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, with the species overwintering as eggs or very young spiders hidden deep in leaf litter and protected spaces.

funFact: These spiders are so small that they can actually become airborne and travel long distances by 'ballooning' - releasing silk threads that catch the wind and carry them through the air like tiny paragliders, sometimes traveling hundreds of miles!
confusionNotes: With only one observation recorded in New England, this species is easily confused with other tiny brown dwarf spiders in the same family. The key is the extremely small size combined with the brownish coloration - if you need a magnifying glass to see it clearly and it's brown rather than black or gray, you might have found this rare little spider.
contextualKnowledge: The family name 'Linyphiidae' comes from the Greek word for 'net,' referring to their web-building abilities. Despite being called 'dwarf' spiders, they're not related to the dwarf spiders in the family Symphytognathidae - this is simply a common name referring to their tiny size.
compareHints: Since this is the only Ceratinella species recorded in New England, compare it with other small brown linyphiids like Erigone species. Ceratinella brunnea tends to be slightly more robust in build compared to the more elongated Erigone spiders, and its brown coloration is warmer in tone. The web structure may also be slightly more substantial despite the spider's tiny size.
